shortDescription.text: The User model's `password` attribute setter is the single place where every credential in the system is transformed before storage.

fullDescription.text: The User model's `password` attribute setter is the single place where every credential in the system is transformed before storage. It calls `security.hash(clearTextPassword)`, which is an unsalted MD5 digest (`lib/insecurity.ts:41`). Because the setter is on the model rather than in a route, every write path — registration, password reset, admin-created accounts, seed data — inherits it, so there is no code path that stores a stronger digest. Two properties make the stored column directly usable to an attacker: MD5 is a fast, GPU-friendly hash with no work factor, and the absence of a per-row salt means identical passwords produce identical digests, so a single rainbow table covers the whole Users table at once. Any read primitive over the database — SQL injection, a leaked backup, a file-read on the co-located SQLite file — converts immediately into cleartext credentials rather than into a cracking problem that costs the attacker time.

shortDescription.text: The repository disables lockfiles outright — the root `.npmrc` and `frontend/.npmrc` both contain a lockfile-disabling directive, `package-lock.json` is listed in `.gitignore:10`, and neither `package-lock.json` nor `frontend/package-lock.json` exists in the tree.

fullDescription.text: The repository disables lockfiles outright — the root `.npmrc` and `frontend/.npmrc` both contain a lockfile-disabling directive, `package-lock.json` is listed in `.gitignore:10`, and neither `package-lock.json` nor `frontend/package-lock.json` exists in the tree. Every build therefore resolves the semver ranges in `package.json` fresh against the registry: `Dockerfile:5` runs `npm install --omit=dev`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml:51` and every test job run bare `npm install`, and `npm ci` appears nowhere in the repository. An attacker who publishes a malicious patch release of any direct or transitive dependency — or who compromises an existing maintainer account — is picked up automatically by the next build. Because `npm install` executes `postinstall` scripts and the docker job publishes the result to `bkimminich/juice-shop:latest` (ci.yml:345), that package's code runs on the runner holding `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` and ships inside the published image to every downstream consumer.

shortDescription.text: The SPA is the token custodian for the whole system.

fullDescription.text: The SPA is the token custodian for the whole system. `login.component.ts:101` receives the raw JWT in the login response body and hands it to browser storage; `request.interceptor.ts:16` then attaches it to every direct call the browser makes to `/api` and `/rest`. No server-side session broker sits between the browser and the API, so the browser holds a long-lived credential that JavaScript must be able to read by design — which is why the storage and guard weaknesses in this component escalate to account takeover rather than staying UI defects. The same architecture forces the SPA to inspect the token itself (`app.guard.ts:38`), leaks the credential into the OAuth URL fragment (`login.component.ts:148`), and leaves nothing to revoke server-side when a token is stolen. A Backend-for-Frontend removes the class: the Express tier exchanges credentials, keeps the API token server-side, and issues the browser only an opaque `HttpOnly` session cookie.

shortDescription.text: The whole datastore is a single plain file — `storage: 'data/juiceshop.sqlite'` — created by the stock `sequelize` sqlite dialect with no page passphrase and no SQLCipher build.

fullDescription.text: The whole datastore is a single plain file — `storage: 'data/juiceshop.sqlite'` — created by the stock `sequelize` sqlite dialect with no page passphrase and no SQLCipher build. It sits inside the application's own working directory, which is also the directory tree the application serves files from, so a path-traversal or arbitrary-file-read primitive anywhere in the shop reads the entire database in one request rather than one row at a time. What that file holds makes the difference material: `models/card.ts:38` stores `cardNum` as a full unmasked `INTEGER` primary account number with no tokenisation or truncation, and `models/user.ts:112` stores `totpSecret` as a plain `STRING` — the shared seed that generates second-factor codes. Neither field is encrypted at the column level either, so there is no defence-in-depth behind the missing file encryption. An attacker who obtains the file gets card numbers they can charge and TOTP seeds that defeat the second factor, without needing to break any cryptography.

shortDescription.text: An attacker who knows any Google-login user's email address can authenticate as that user without touching Google.

fullDescription.text: An attacker who knows any Google-login user's email address can authenticate as that user without touching Google. On the OAuth callback, `oauth.component.ts:30` computes `const password = btoa(profile.email.split('').reverse().join(''))` and registers the account with it via `userService.save()`, then `login()` at line 46 reuses the same derivation to sign in through the ordinary `/rest/user/login` password endpoint. The derivation is a public, deterministic function of a public identifier: base64 of the reversed email. Every OAuth account therefore also has a working local password that the attacker can compute offline, which makes the password endpoint a parallel authentication path around the federated flow entirely — MFA, Google account recovery, and the `authorizedRedirects` allowlist all sit on the other path and never see the request.

shortDescription.text: The RSA private key used to sign every session JWT is a literal PEM block in `lib/insecurity.ts`, committed to a public repository.

fullDescription.text: The RSA private key used to sign every session JWT is a literal PEM block in `lib/insecurity.ts`, committed to a public repository. `authorize()` signs with that constant and the matching public key ships as `encryptionkeys/jwt.pub`, so the signing secret is available to anyone who can read the source or pull the published container image. An attacker constructs a payload of their choosing — `{"data": {"id": 1, "email": "admin@juice-sh.op", "role": "admin"}}` — signs it with the copied key using RS256, and presents it as a Bearer token. Every server-side check that only verifies the signature accepts it. The same constant is reused as the HMAC key for `deluxeToken()` at line 150, so the deluxe-membership token that `isDeluxe()` cross-checks is forgeable from the same material.

shortDescription.text: Every server-side token check omits an algorithm allow-list.

fullDescription.text: Every server-side token check omits an algorithm allow-list. `isAuthorized()` constructs the express-jwt middleware with only `{ secret: publicKey }`; `updateAuthenticatedUsers()` on line 189 calls `jwt.verify(token, publicKey, cb)` with no options object; and `verify()` on line 55 hands the public key to `jws.verify` in the algorithm parameter. The pinned dependency versions — express-jwt 0.1.3 and jsonwebtoken 0.4.0 in package.json — predate algorithm enforcement, so the header's `alg` field decides which verification routine runs. An attacker sets the header algorithm to `none`, strips the signature, and supplies an arbitrary payload; alternatively they switch to a symmetric HMAC algorithm and sign with the published `encryptionkeys/jwt.pub` contents, which the code passes as the verification secret. Both variants yield a token the middleware treats as authentic.

shortDescription.text: Without an explicit algorithm allowlist, attackers can forge tokens with alg:none (older lib versions) or use the public key as an HMAC secret to mint valid signatures.

fullDescription.text: Without an explicit algorithm allowlist, attackers can forge tokens with alg:none (older lib versions) or use the public key as an HMAC secret to mint valid signatures.

shortDescription.text: An attacker submits a feedback comment containing markup and waits for an administrator to open the admin panel.

fullDescription.text: An attacker submits a feedback comment containing markup and waits for an administrator to open the admin panel. `findAllFeedbacks()` at `frontend/src/app/administration/administration.component.ts:91` passes each `feedback.comment` straight through `this.sanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml()`, and `administration.component.html:60` renders the result into `[innerHTML]`. The bypass call disables the only escaping Angular would otherwise apply, so the stored comment executes in the administrator's origin. The same pattern sits two methods above at line 73, where `user.email` is wrapped in a `<span>` and bypassed for the user table rendered at `administration.component.html:26` and `:113` — a registered attacker controls that email string. Payloads run with the administrator's session, and since the JWT lives in `localStorage` (see the token-storage finding) a single script tag both exfiltrates the admin bearer token and issues authenticated calls to `/api/Users` on the admin's behalf.

shortDescription.text: The login handler builds its credential lookup by string interpolation: the raw `req.body.email` value is pasted into a `SELECT * FROM Users WHERE email = '...' AND password = '...'` statement and executed through Sequelize's raw-query API with `plain: true`.

fullDescription.text: The login handler builds its credential lookup by string interpolation: the raw `req.body.email` value is pasted into a `SELECT * FROM Users WHERE email = '...' AND password = '...'` statement and executed through Sequelize's raw-query API with `plain: true`. An unauthenticated attacker posting `{"email": "' OR 1=1--", "password": "x"}` to POST /rest/user/login terminates the email literal and comments out the entire password comparison, so the query returns the first row of the Users table. The handler then treats that row as a verified user and calls `security.authorize()` on it, minting a signed 6-hour RS256 JWT for whichever account is returned — in the seeded dataset, the admin. The same primitive supports UNION-based extraction of every column of the Users table, including the MD5 password hashes and TOTP secrets.

shortDescription.text: The login handler builds its authentication query by interpolating `req.body.email` and the MD5 digest of `req.body.password` directly into a raw SQL string passed to Sequelize's `query()` with `plain: true`.

fullDescription.text: The login handler builds its authentication query by interpolating `req.body.email` and the MD5 digest of `req.body.password` directly into a raw SQL string passed to Sequelize's `query()` with `plain: true`. No parameter binding, escaping, or type check stands between the JSON request body and the SQLite parser. An unauthenticated attacker POSTs to `/rest/user/login` with an email of `' OR true--`, which terminates the string literal and comments out the password comparison, so the first row of `Users` is returned as the authenticated principal. Because `plain: true` returns exactly one row and the seeded admin is row 1, the attacker receives a valid RS256 JWT for the administrator without ever knowing a password. The same sink also permits UNION-based extraction of any table SQLite can reach.

shortDescription.text: Server-side authorization MUST derive the resource owner from the authenticated session (req.user / req.session / req.auth), never from attacker-controlled request data.

fullDescription.text: Server-side authorization MUST derive the resource owner from the authenticated session (req.user / req.session / req.auth), never from attacker-controlled request data. Trusting req.body.UserId etc. enables horizontal privilege escalation across all authenticated tenants.

shortDescription.text: extractZipBuffer() at routes/fileUpload.ts:28-36 iterates every archive entry and writes it with the raw, attacker-controlled entry.path concatenated onto the literal prefix 'uploads/complaints/'.

fullDescription.text: extractZipBuffer() at routes/fileUpload.ts:28-36 iterates every archive entry and writes it with the raw, attacker-controlled entry.path concatenated onto the literal prefix 'uploads/complaints/'. The only guard is absolutePath.includes(path.resolve('.')) on line 33, which merely asserts that the resolved target lies somewhere beneath the repository root - it does not assert that it lies beneath uploads/complaints/. An entry named ../../ftp/legal.md resolves to <repo>/ftp/legal.md, passes the includes() check, and is written. Because the write on line 34 uses the un-normalised relative concatenation rather than the validated absolutePath, an attacker can place files anywhere in the application directory: overwrite ftp/legal.md, drop a file into the publicly served frontend/dist/frontend tree, or clobber a .ts/.js source file that the process will load on the next restart. The endpoint is anonymous (see file-upload-service-002), so no account is needed.

shortDescription.text: handleXmlUpload passes the raw uploaded buffer to parseXmlString at routes/fileUpload.ts:76.

fullDescription.text: handleXmlUpload passes the raw uploaded buffer to parseXmlString at routes/fileUpload.ts:76. lib/xml.ts:36 configures libxml2 with XML_PARSE_NOENT | XML_PARSE_DTDLOAD and lib/xml.ts:22 calls xmlRegisterFsInputProviders(), which grants the WASM parser host filesystem access. An uploaded document declaring <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd"> therefore has the entity substituted during parsing. The parsed result is not discarded: line 79 embeds utils.trunc(xmlString, 400) directly into the Error message handed to next(), so the first 400 characters of the resolved entity are returned to the uploader in the error response body. Because the same parser accepts http:// and ftp:// system identifiers, the same request doubles as a server-side request forgery primitive against services reachable from the application host. The endpoint is anonymous, so this is a pre-auth read primitive.

shortDescription.text: The B2B order handler takes the `orderLinesData` field straight from the JSON request body and evaluates it as JavaScript.

fullDescription.text: The B2B order handler takes the `orderLinesData` field straight from the JSON request body and evaluates it as JavaScript. The string is placed into a `vm` context together with the `notevil` evaluator and executed by `vm.runInContext('safeEval(orderLinesData)', sandbox, { timeout: 2000 })`. Neither `node:vm` nor `notevil` is a security boundary: `node:vm` shares the host realm and is documented as unsuitable for untrusted code, and `notevil` is an interpreter with a public history of prototype- and constructor-based escapes. Any authenticated caller — and registration is open at server.ts:408 — can therefore run attacker-chosen expressions inside the API process. The 2-second timeout only bounds a runaway loop; it does not constrain what a fast payload reaches.

shortDescription.text: User registration is exposed through the generic Sequelize REST layer at `POST /api/Users`.

fullDescription.text: User registration is exposed through the generic Sequelize REST layer at `POST /api/Users`. The only pre-handler middleware (server.ts:408-422) trims `email`, `password` and `passwordRepeat` and runs challenge checks; nothing removes unexpected fields, so every attribute declared on the model is writable from the request body. The `role` attribute at models/user.ts:79 defaults to `customer` but its validator accepts the literal `admin`, and its setter simply stores whatever it is given. A self-registering attacker therefore includes `"role": "admin"` in the signup body and receives an administrator account. The same primitive sets `deluxeToken`, `lastLoginIp` and `isActive`, so an attacker can also fabricate the deluxe entitlement or reactivate a disabled account.

shortDescription.text: Server code that consumes req.body.role / req.body.isAdmin / etc.

fullDescription.text: Server code that consumes req.body.role / req.body.isAdmin / etc. without an explicit allowlist trusts the client to behave. An attacker simply adds {"role":"admin"} to their request to escalate.

shortDescription.text: An attacker targets the Google sign-in path.

fullDescription.text: An attacker targets the Google sign-in path. `googleLogin()` at `frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:148` navigates the browser to `accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/v2/auth` with `response_type=token` — the deprecated implicit flow — and no `state`, no `nonce`, and no PKCE parameters (repo-wide grep for `code_challenge`, `code_verifier`, `state=`, `nonce` across `frontend/src` returns zero hits). Google therefore returns a live access token in the URL fragment, which `parseRedirectUrlParams()` at `frontend/src/app/oauth/oauth.component.ts:71` splits out of `this.route.snapshot.data.params` and posts to `/rest/user/login`. Because the fragment is part of the address bar, the token reaches browser history, screenshots, and any injected script on the callback page. The absent `state` parameter is the second half: an attacker who obtains a token for their own Google account can hand a victim a crafted `#access_token=<attacker_token>` callback link, and the SPA logs the victim into the attacker's account without any binding check.

shortDescription.text: POST /rest/user/login accepts unlimited attempts.

fullDescription.text: POST /rest/user/login accepts unlimited attempts. The route is registered with no rate limiter — unlike /rest/user/reset-password and the three /rest/2fa endpoints, which each carry an express-rate-limit instance — and the handler itself implements no failed-attempt counter, no per-account lockout, no exponential backoff, and no CAPTCHA. A grep for any throttling or attempt-counting identifier in routes/login.ts and lib/insecurity.ts returns zero hits. An attacker therefore runs credential stuffing against the full user list obtained from routes/authenticatedUsers.ts at whatever rate the network allows, and each attempt costs the server only one MD5 computation, so there is no natural throttle either. Because no authentication event is logged, the campaign is also invisible.

shortDescription.text: Password recovery requires only an email address and the answer to a security question.

fullDescription.text: Password recovery requires only an email address and the answer to a security question. There is no emailed one-time link, no possession proof, no notification to the account owner, and no session invalidation. The handler compares `security.hmac(answer)` against the stored answer and, on a match, immediately writes the caller-supplied `new` password onto the user record. Security answers are inherently low-entropy — the seeded dataset uses values such as a family member's name or a childhood street — so an attacker who knows or can research the victim (or who simply enumerates common answers) takes over the account outright. Because the reset succeeds silently, the legitimate owner learns of it only when their own password stops working.

shortDescription.text: The password-change handler makes the current-password check conditional on the client having sent one: `if (currentPassword && security.hash(currentPassword) !== loggedInUser.data.password)`.

fullDescription.text: The password-change handler makes the current-password check conditional on the client having sent one: `if (currentPassword && security.hash(currentPassword) !== loggedInUser.data.password)`. When `current` is simply omitted from the query string the condition short-circuits and the update at line 51 proceeds, so possession of a bearer token alone is sufficient to set a new password. That removes the last barrier that would otherwise contain a stolen or forged token — and this component offers several ways to obtain one, including the algorithm-confusion path at lib/insecurity.ts:52. The endpoint is additionally registered as a GET (server.ts:597), so the new password travels in the URL and is written to the access log that routes/logfileServer.ts:14 serves to anonymous callers.

shortDescription.text: An attacker who can research or guess the answer can satisfy the recovery check and take over the account without the original credential.

fullDescription.text: An attacker who can research or guess the answer can satisfy the recovery check and take over the account without the original credential.

shortDescription.text: The middleware chain for POST /file-upload (server.ts:309) is uploadToMemory.single('file') -> ensureFileIsPassed -> observeFileUploadMetricsMiddleware -> checkUploadSize -> checkFileType -> handleZipFileUpload -> handleXmlUpload -> handleYamlUpload.

fullDescription.text: The middleware chain for POST /file-upload (server.ts:309) is uploadToMemory.single('file') -> ensureFileIsPassed -> observeFileUploadMetricsMiddleware -> checkUploadSize -> checkFileType -> handleZipFileUpload -> handleXmlUpload -> handleYamlUpload. None of these establishes or checks a caller identity: ensureFileIsPassed (routes/fileUpload.ts:19) only asserts that a multipart part was present, and routes/fileUpload.ts imports no authentication helper at all. server.ts uses security.isAuthorized() on 23 other routes, so the omission here is specific to the upload surface rather than a global design. Every downstream weakness in this component - Zip Slip write, XXE file read, decompression bomb - is therefore reachable by an anonymous internet client with a single curl request, and no user account, session, or token has to be obtained first. The absence of an identity also means the metrics and error paths record no principal, so the uploads cannot be attributed after the fact.

shortDescription.text: An attacker mints a JWT whose payload contains the victim's numeric user id, signs it with any key of their choosing, and sends it as the `Authorization` header on `POST /rest/chat`.

fullDescription.text: An attacker mints a JWT whose payload contains the victim's numeric user id, signs it with any key of their choosing, and sends it as the `Authorization` header on `POST /rest/chat`. `getUserId()` at `routes/chat.ts:45` resolves the identity with `security.decode(token)`, which is `jws.decode(token)?.payload` at `lib/insecurity.ts:56` — the payload is base64-decoded and returned with no signature check, while the verifying counterpart `security.verify()` (line 55) is never called on this path. The forged id then drives two security decisions in the same handler: `getUserNameFromToken()` writes the victim's username into the system prompt (line 83), and the `getOrderById` tool loads the victim's email to authorize order lookups (lines 159-169). The attacker holds the agent's full user context without ever authenticating.

shortDescription.text: The Socket.IO server is created with `new Server(server, { cors: { origin: 'http://localhost:4200' } })` and immediately registers `io.on('connection', ...)` with no `io.use()` handshake middleware.

fullDescription.text: The Socket.IO server is created with `new Server(server, { cors: { origin: 'http://localhost:4200' } })` and immediately registers `io.on('connection', ...)` with no `io.use()` handshake middleware. Nothing reads `socket.handshake.auth`, `socket.handshake.headers.cookie`, or the JWT that `security.isAuthorized()` validates on the REST side, so the socket never acquires an identity. Because the Socket.IO server is attached to the same HTTP server as the Express API (server.ts:749), an anonymous internet client that can reach port 3000 can open the WebSocket upgrade and immediately invoke every registered event handler. The CORS `origin` value is not a substitute: Socket.IO only enforces it against browsers that send an `Origin` header, and any non-browser client (curl, socket.io-client, a script) connects regardless. This is the WebSocket leg of the same trust boundary the REST API guards with expressJwt.

shortDescription.text: Security answers are the fallback authenticator for the password-reset flow, so a digest an attacker can invert is equivalent to a stored password.

fullDescription.text: Security answers are the fallback authenticator for the password-reset flow, so a digest an attacker can invert is equivalent to a stored password. The SecurityAnswer model protects them with `security.hmac(answer)`, which is HMAC-SHA256 under the literal key `pa4qacea4VK9t9nGv7yZtwmj` compiled into `lib/insecurity.ts:42`. Three defects compound here. The key is a source-code constant in a public repository, so it provides no secrecy against anyone who can read the project. HMAC-SHA256 is a single fast round with no work factor, so it is a poor choice for a low-entropy secret regardless of key handling. And the construction is deterministic without a per-row salt, so equal answers yield equal digests and one precomputed table covers every user. Security answers draw from a small space — a pet name, a city, a mother's maiden name — so a wordlist of a few hundred thousand entries inverts essentially the whole SecurityAnswers table.

shortDescription.text: POST /rest/web3/walletNFTVerify reads req.body.walletAddress at routes/nftMint.ts:41 and treats the string as proof that the caller controls that Ethereum account.

fullDescription.text: POST /rest/web3/walletNFTVerify reads req.body.walletAddress at routes/nftMint.ts:41 and treats the string as proof that the caller controls that Ethereum account. There is no session authentication on the route (server.ts:644 registers it without security.isAuthorized()) and no cryptographic ownership proof — a grep across the component for verifyMessage, recoverAddress, SiweMessage or signature returns zero hits. Ethereum addresses are public data emitted by the NFTMinted event the server itself subscribes to at routes/nftMint.ts:24, so any anonymous internet caller who observes or guesses a minter address can claim it. The same handler then calls addressesMinted.delete(metamaskAddress) at line 43 before granting credit, so the impersonation is also destructive: the legitimate minter's pending entry is consumed and their own later verification returns 'Wallet did not mint the NFT'.

shortDescription.text: GET /redirect?to=<url> gates the redirect on security.isRedirectAllowed(), which loops the allowlist and accepts the URL when url.includes(allowedUrl) is true anywhere in the string (lib/insecurity.ts:136).

fullDescription.text: GET /redirect?to=<url> gates the redirect on security.isRedirectAllowed(), which loops the allowlist and accepts the URL when url.includes(allowedUrl) is true anywhere in the string (lib/insecurity.ts:136). Because the check is an unanchored substring test rather than an origin comparison, an attacker appends an allowlisted URL to their own domain as a fragment or query value — https://attacker.example/steal#https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop — and routes/redirect.ts:19 hands the browser a 302 to the attacker host. The redirect runs on the shop's own origin, so the link carries the shop's domain in mail filters, chat previews and user inspection, which is exactly what makes it useful for credential phishing. The same primitive is the classic sink for OAuth authorization-code and token theft whenever an authorization server or SSO flow is configured to return to a shop URL.

shortDescription.text: The amount credited to a user's wallet is chosen in the browser and never re-derived server-side.

fullDescription.text: The amount credited to a user's wallet is chosen in the browser and never re-derived server-side. `wallet.component.ts:44` writes the top-up amount from `balanceControl` into `sessionStorage.walletTotal` and routes to the payment screen; `payment.component.ts:131` reads it back as `this.totalPrice`; `payment.component.ts:218` then posts `walletService.put({ balance: this.totalPrice, paymentId: this.paymentId })`. The only bound on the value is the Angular validator pair `Validators.min(10)` and `Validators.max(1000)` declared on the form control at `wallet.component.ts:30`, which runs in the browser and never sees the request. The server accepts the number as given: `addWalletBalance()` at `routes/wallet.ts:22-28` checks only that the refe**** (10 chars) card belongs to the caller, then calls `WalletModel.increment({ balance: req.body.balance })` with no range check and without charging the card for the amount. An attacker who edits the `sessionStorage` value between the two screens — or who posts to the endpoint directly — credits their wallet with an arbitrary balance and spends it in the same checkout flow.

shortDescription.text: Nothing in the delivered page restricts where script may come from or where it may send data.

fullDescription.text: Nothing in the delivered page restricts where script may come from or where it may send data. `frontend/src/index.html` ships no `Content-Security-Policy` meta tag, and a repo-wide grep for `Content-Security-Policy` across `frontend/src` returns zero hits. With nine active sanitizer bypasses in the SPA — `administration.component.ts:73` and `:91`, `search-result.component.ts:110` and `:143`, `about.component.ts:119`, `track-result.component.ts:48`, `last-login-ip.component.ts:39`, `data-export.component.ts:57`, `score-board.component.ts:82` — the absence removes the last barrier between an injected payload and an outbound request: an XSS payload may load remote script and `fetch()` the `localStorage` token to any host it chooses. The page also carries an inline `<script>` block at `index.html:17` that initialises the cookie-consent widget, so adopting a strict policy requires moving that block to a file or hashing it first.

shortDescription.text: GET /rest/saveLoginIp records the caller's `true-client-ip` request header verbatim into the user's `lastLoginIp` column.

fullDescription.text: GET /rest/saveLoginIp records the caller's `true-client-ip` request header verbatim into the user's `lastLoginIp` column. The header is fully attacker-controlled — there is no proxy that overwrites it and no format check that the value resembles an IP address. Sanitization is conditional: `security.sanitizeSecure()` runs only in the `else` branch, so whenever the corresponding challenge flag is enabled the raw header value is written straight to the database. Any authenticated user can therefore store an HTML payload such as an `iframe` with a `javascript:` source in their own record. The value is later rendered wherever last-login IPs are displayed, notably the administrative user list served by routes/authenticatedUsers.ts, so the payload executes in an administrator's browser with the administrator's session.

shortDescription.text: The Socket.IO server accepts every connection without any handshake authentication: there is no middleware on the namespace, no token is read from the handshake, and no user identity is bound to the socket.

fullDescription.text: The Socket.IO server accepts every connection without any handshake authentication: there is no middleware on the namespace, no token is read from the handshake, and no user identity is bound to the socket. On connect the server immediately pushes the entire `notifications` array to the client. The `notification received` handler then lets any connected client splice entries out of that shared server-side array by flag value, and the `verifySvgInjectionChallenge` / `verifyLocalXssChallenge` handlers accept arbitrary client payloads that drive server state. The CORS origin is pinned to `http://localhost:4200`, which restricts browser-based cross-origin use but places no restriction at all on a non-browser client such as a socket.io CLI or a script setting its own Origin header.

shortDescription.text: A request-controlled path with `../` can read arbitrary files (/etc/passwd, source, secrets) or write outside the intended root.

fullDescription.text: A request-controlled path with `../` can read arbitrary files (/etc/passwd, source, secrets) or write outside the intended root.

shortDescription.text: Zip entries are written using the archive's own entry name with no normalisation.

fullDescription.text: Zip entries are written using the archive's own entry name with no normalisation. routes/fileUpload.ts:31 resolves `'uploads/complaints/' + fileName`, and the guard on line 33 only asserts that the resolved path is inside the process working directory — an entry named `../../ftp/legal.md` satisfies that check while still escaping the intended upload directory. Worse, the write on line 34 does not use the resolved path at all; it concatenates the raw entry name into `fs.createWriteStream`, so traversal segments are honoured by the filesystem regardless of what the guard computed. Because `/file-upload` is registered without authentication (server.ts:309), an anonymous client can overwrite any file the application user can write, including files served from `ftp/` and the SQLite database.

shortDescription.text: The shared XML parser enables entity substitution and DTD loading and then explicitly grants the WASM parser host filesystem access.

fullDescription.text: The shared XML parser enables entity substitution and DTD loading and then explicitly grants the WASM parser host filesystem access. lib/xml.ts:35 combines `XML_PARSE_NOENT` with `XML_PARSE_DTDLOAD`, and lib/xml.ts:22 calls `xmlRegisterFsInputProviders()` so that `file://` system entities resolve against the container filesystem. The reachable caller is the upload handler: routes/fileUpload.ts:76 passes the uploaded buffer to `parseXmlString`, and line 79 places the expanded document into an error message that the error handler returns to the client. The attacker therefore both triggers the read and receives its contents. The upload route at server.ts:309 carries no authentication middleware, so the whole chain is available to an anonymous client.

shortDescription.text: The review update handler passes `req.body.id` straight into a Mongo-style selector as `{ _id: req.body.id }` and issues the update with `{ multi: true }`.

fullDescription.text: The review update handler passes `req.body.id` straight into a Mongo-style selector as `{ _id: req.body.id }` and issues the update with `{ multi: true }`. Because the body is parsed JSON, the attacker controls the type of that field, not just its value: sending an object such as `{"$ne": ""}` turns the selector into a predicate that matches every stored review, and `multi: true` applies the update to all of them in one request. The handler also reads the authenticated user at line 16 but never uses it in the selector, so no ownership predicate limits the rows either. The route requires a token (server.ts:634), which open registration makes trivial to obtain.

shortDescription.text: The `heroku` job pipes a remote script straight into a shell: `.github/workflows/ci.yml:358` runs `curl https://cli-assets.heroku.com/install.sh | sh` with no checksum, no signature, and no version pin.

fullDescription.text: The `heroku` job pipes a remote script straight into a shell: `.github/workflows/ci.yml:358` runs `curl https://cli-assets.heroku.com/install.sh | sh` with no checksum, no signature, and no version pin. Whatever bytes `cli-assets.heroku.com` returns at that moment execute as the runner user. The same job then hands `secrets.HEROKU_API_KEY` to the deploy step at ci.yml:371, and the job runs on every push to `master` and `develop`. An attacker who controls that host, its CDN edge, or the DNS answer for it — or a Heroku-side compromise — gains code execution on a runner holding a production deployment credential.

shortDescription.text: Most workflows in this repository pin third-party actions to 40-character commit SHAs, but six references do not.

fullDescription.text: Most workflows in this repository pin third-party actions to 40-character commit SHAs, but six references do not. The worst is `.github/workflows/image_actions.yml:33`, which uses `calibreapp/image-actions@main` — a branch ref that resolves to whatever the upstream maintainer last pushed, and which receives `secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN` at line 35. The same file uses `actions/checkout@v6` (line 30) and `peter-evans/create-pull-request@v8` (line 42); `.github/workflows/ci.yml:188` uses `coverallsapp/github-action@v2` with `secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN`; `.github/workflows/codeql-analysis.yml:23,34,36` use `github/codeql-action/*@v3` in a job holding `security-events: write`. Git tags and branches are mutable, so an upstream account takeover silently replaces the code executed inside these jobs — the SHA-pinning control the pipeline otherwise relies on simply is not applied here.

shortDescription.text: checkFileType (routes/fileUpload.ts:62-68) and checkUploadSize (routes/fileUpload.ts:55-60) are registered in the POST /file-upload chain and read like validation, but neither ever short-circuits the request: both consist solely of a challengeUtils.solveIf() call followed by an unconditional next().

fullDescription.text: checkFileType (routes/fileUpload.ts:62-68) and checkUploadSize (routes/fileUpload.ts:55-60) are registered in the POST /file-upload chain and read like validation, but neither ever short-circuits the request: both consist solely of a challengeUtils.solveIf() call followed by an unconditional next(). checkFileType computes the extension on line 63 and on line 64 uses it only to decide whether to mark a training challenge solved - a file with an extension outside {pdf, xml, zip, yml, yaml} is passed straight through rather than rejected. The extension itself is derived from the client-supplied originalname and is never cross-checked against the buffer's magic bytes, so the ZIP, XML, and YAML handlers dispatch purely on an attacker-chosen suffix. The practical result is that the endpoint accepts any content of any type up to the 200000-byte multer limit, and the routing decision between the three parser paths is under attacker control.

shortDescription.text: LLM01 / ASI01 — Prompt Injection.

fullDescription.text: LLM01 / ASI01 — Prompt Injection. `routes/chat.ts:191` takes `req.body?.messages` and forwards the array unchanged into `streamText({ system, messages, tools })` at lines 203-207. No schema validates the element shape and no filter restricts the `role` field, so the client is not limited to `role: 'user'` turns. An attacker posts a body containing a fabricated `role: 'assistant'` turn in which the assistant already agreed to the coupon, or an extra `role: 'system'` turn that revokes the ceiling in `buildSystemPrompt()`. Because the transcript is reconstructed entirely from client input on every request, the server holds no authoritative conversation state to contradict the forgery — the model plans its next tool call against attacker-authored history.

shortDescription.text: The persistence layer, not the view layer, is where this application decides whether user content is safe to render.

fullDescription.text: The persistence layer, not the view layer, is where this application decides whether user content is safe to render. Three model setters strip markup on the way into the database — `username` (models/user.ts:47), `Feedback.comment` (models/feedback.ts:41), and `Product.description` (models/product.ts:44) — and each of them branches on a runtime flag. When `utils.isChallengeEnabled(...)` is true, `username` is passed through `security.sanitizeLegacy` and `comment` through `security.sanitizeHtml`; only the `else` branch reaches `security.sanitizeSecure`. That inverts the safe default: the weaker sanitizer is the active path in the deployed configuration, and the stronger one runs only when the flag is off. The architectural problem outlives the flag, though. Sanitising once at write time means the stored value is trusted forever after, so the same row is emitted verbatim into HTML, into an Angular binding, into a JSON response, and into a PDF — contexts with different escaping rules that a single input-time filter cannot satisfy. A payload that survives one sanitiser pass is then persistent and served to every viewer under the shop's own origin.

shortDescription.text: Coupons minted by the agent leave no attributable record.

fullDescription.text: Coupons minted by the agent leave no attributable record. `security.generateCoupon(discount)` at `routes/chat.ts:184` returns the code to the caller and writes nothing: the only observable trace is `metricToolCalls.labels({ tool })` at line 227, a Prometheus counter labelled by tool name alone with no user, no discount value, and no timestamp. The `logger` is invoked at exactly two places in the file — lines 211 and 263, both LLM transport errors — so no security event is ever written, and `lib/insecurity.ts` contains no logging at all. When a 50% coupon is redeemed at checkout, the operator can establish that some coupon-tool call happened during the day but cannot tie it to a session, an account, or a discount value, so neither the abuse nor a legitimate issuance can be reconstructed or disputed.

shortDescription.text: The session JWT is kept where any script in the origin can read it.

fullDescription.text: The session JWT is kept where any script in the origin can read it. `login.component.ts:101`, `oauth.component.ts:51`, `payment.component.ts:232`, and `two-factor-auth-enter.component.ts:56` all write the token with `localStorage.setItem('token', ...)`, and `request.interceptor.ts:16` reads it back on every outgoing request to build the `Authorization: Bearer` header. The pre-authentication 2FA token is held the same way (`two-factor-auth-service.ts:38` reads `totp_tmp_token` from `localStorage`). The token is additionally mirrored into a cookie at `login.component.ts:104` with only an `expires` option — a grep for `httpOnly`, `secure:`, or `sameSite` across `frontend/src/app` returns zero hits, so that copy is JavaScript-readable, is sent cross-site, and travels in cleartext wherever the deployment is not HTTPS (`environment.ts:12` points `hostServer` at `http://localhost:3000`). Any of the nine sanitizer bypasses in this component turns into full credential theft with a one-line payload, and the stolen token stays valid until its own expiry because there is no server-side session to revoke.

shortDescription.text: GET /rest/user/authentication-details calls `UserModel.findAll()` with no filter and spreads each row's `dataValues` into the response.

fullDescription.text: GET /rest/user/authentication-details calls `UserModel.findAll()` with no filter and spreads each row's `dataValues` into the response. Only two fields are redacted — `password` and `totpSecret` are replaced with asterisks — so every other column ships in full: email, username, role, `deluxeToken`, `lastLoginIp`, `profileImage`, `isActive`, and the numeric primary key. The route is mounted behind the shared authorization middleware but carries no role check, so any customer-level session enumerates the entire user base, learns which accounts hold the admin or accounting role, and reads the `deluxeToken` values used by `isDeluxe()`. The handler additionally derives `lastLoginTime` from the in-memory token map, which reveals exactly which accounts currently hold a live session — a direct targeting aid.

shortDescription.text: Security-question answers are protected by `hmac()`, an HMAC-SHA256 whose key is the string literal `pa4qacea4VK9t9nGv7yZtwmj` embedded in the source.

fullDescription.text: Security-question answers are protected by `hmac()`, an HMAC-SHA256 whose key is the string literal `pa4qacea4VK9t9nGv7yZtwmj` embedded in the source. Because the key is public and the same for every user, the construction provides no more protection than an unkeyed hash: an attacker who obtains the SecurityAnswer table — for example through the login SQL injection — precomputes HMACs for a dictionary of plausible answers and matches them offline, with no per-user salt to force separate work per account. Recovered answers feed straight into the reset-password flow, so cracking the table converts into mass account takeover. The recovered key is also usable to forge a matching answer value directly if write access to the table is obtained.

shortDescription.text: Passwords are stored as a single unsalted MD5 digest.

fullDescription.text: Passwords are stored as a single unsalted MD5 digest. The exported `hash()` helper is a bare MD5 of the cleartext, and the User model's password setter calls it on every write, so every row in the Users table holds a raw MD5 value. MD5 is fast to compute and unsalted digests are identical across users, so an attacker who obtains the table — trivially, via the login SQL injection in routes/login.ts — recovers plaintext passwords by rainbow-table lookup for common values and by GPU brute force for the rest, at rates measured in billions of guesses per second. Identical hashes also reveal which users share a password. The same `hash()` function additionally gates 2FA setup and 2FA disable in routes/2fa.ts, so cracking one password removes the victim's second factor as well.

shortDescription.text: `serveLogFiles` sends any file under `logs/` to any caller.

fullDescription.text: `serveLogFiles` sends any file under `logs/` to any caller. The only check is that the requested name contains no forward slash (line 13); there is no authentication, no authorization, and no extension allowlist. The directory it exposes holds the Morgan `combined` access log written at server.ts:338, which records full request lines. Because several sensitive operations in this component are GET requests that carry their parameters in the query string — most notably `/rest/user/change-password?current=...&new=...` at routes/changePassword.ts:14 — the access log contains plaintext passwords alongside the bearer-token-bearing requests that produced them. The route also sits next to a directory index (`/support/logs`, server.ts:281), so an attacker does not need to guess filenames.

shortDescription.text: The profile-image-by-URL handler fetches whatever URL the request body carries: `const url = req.body.imageUrl` at line 19 followed by `await fetch(url)` at line 24.

fullDescription.text: The profile-image-by-URL handler fetches whatever URL the request body carries: `const url = req.body.imageUrl` at line 19 followed by `await fetch(url)` at line 24. No scheme allowlist, host allowlist, DNS resolution check, or redirect limit is applied, so the request originates from inside the application's network position. An authenticated user can therefore reach cloud instance metadata endpoints, container-internal services, and any host reachable from the API that is not reachable from the internet. The response body is streamed to disk under `frontend/dist/.../uploads/<userId>.<ext>` and served back as the user's profile image, which turns the SSRF into a read primitive rather than a blind one. On fetch failure the handler falls back to storing the raw URL as the profile image (line 36), which is itself the value interpolated into the Content-Security-Policy header at routes/userProfile.ts:88.

shortDescription.text: Static, long-lived credentials are placed in the environment of jobs that also execute unverified third-party code.

fullDescription.text: Static, long-lived credentials are placed in the environment of jobs that also execute unverified third-party code. `.github/workflows/ci.yml:327` passes `secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` to the docker login step of a job that ran `actions/checkout` without `persist-credentials: false`; `ci.yml:249-253` hands `E2E_SOLUTIONS_WEBHOOK`, `ALCHEMY_API_KEY`, `CYPRESS_RECORD_KEY` and `GITHUB_TOKEN` to the Cypress job, which first runs `npm install` over unpinned dependencies with install scripts enabled and then boots the full application; `update-challenges-www.yml:19` and `update-news-www.yml:14` expose `BOT_TOKEN`, a cross-repository write credential. Any code that executes in those jobs — a compromised npm postinstall hook, a repointed action — reads the environment and the checkout credentials in `.git/config` directly. Because the Docker Hub and bot tokens are static personal access tokens rather than short-lived OIDC credentials, a single leak stays usable until someone notices and rotates it.

shortDescription.text: GitHub Actions workflow-level permissions block: Without an explicit permissions block, the workflow inherits the repository default (commonly write-all) for GITHUB_TOKEN — any compromised step can push code, create releases, or approve PRs.

fullDescription.text: GitHub Actions workflow-level permissions block: Without an explicit permissions block, the workflow inherits the repository default (commonly write-all) for GITHUB_TOKEN — any compromised step can push code, create releases, or approve PRs. Found in .github/workflows/ci.yml:1.

fullDescription.text: Third-party GitHub Actions pinned to commit SHA: Tag-based action references (@v3, @main) are mutable — a compromised publisher can retroactively inject malicious code into an already-used tag. Found in .github/workflows/ci.yml:188.

shortDescription.text: servePublicFiles() validates the requested filename against an allow-list of .md and .pdf at routes/fileServer.ts:27, and only afterwards, on line 28, calls security.cutOffPoisonNullByte(file), which truncates the string at the first %00 (lib/insecurity.ts:44-49).

fullDescription.text: servePublicFiles() validates the requested filename against an allow-list of .md and .pdf at routes/fileServer.ts:27, and only afterwards, on line 28, calls security.cutOffPoisonNullByte(file), which truncates the string at the first %00 (lib/insecurity.ts:44-49). Validation therefore runs on the pre-truncation string and the filesystem read on line 33 runs on the post-truncation string, so the two disagree by construction. A request for /ftp/incident-support.kdbx%2500.md satisfies the allow-list as '...kdbx%00.md' and then resolves to ftp/incident-support.kdbx. The ftp/ directory holds a KeePass database (incident-support.kdbx), a full package-lock.json.bak dependency inventory, a compiled encrypt.pyc, and coupons_2013.md.bak - none of which the .md/.pdf policy is meant to release. The route requires no authentication, and serveIndex on server.ts:269 publishes the directory listing that tells the attacker exactly which names to ask for.

shortDescription.text: server.ts:277 mounts serveIndex on /encryptionkeys with `{ icons: true, view: 'details' }`, publishing a browsable listing of the key material directory, and server.ts:278 mounts serveKeyFiles() so any name in that listing can be fetched.

fullDescription.text: server.ts:277 mounts serveIndex on /encryptionkeys with `{ icons: true, view: 'details' }`, publishing a browsable listing of the key material directory, and server.ts:278 mounts serveKeyFiles() so any name in that listing can be fetched. routes/keyServer.ts:9-19 applies exactly one check - that the name contains no forward slash - before res.sendFile(path.resolve('encryptionkeys/', file)) on line 14. There is no authentication, no extension allow-list, and no distinction between key material that is safe to publish and key material that is not: the directory currently holds jwt.pub (the RSA public key used to verify session tokens, benign on its own) and premium.key. Publishing the token-verification public key hands an attacker the exact modulus and exponent needed to test offline whether the deployment accepts an alg:none or HS256-confusion token signed with that public key as the HMAC secret, and the directory listing guarantees that any key file added here in the future is discovered immediately.

shortDescription.text: LLM07 — System Prompt Leakage.

fullDescription.text: LLM07 — System Prompt Leakage. `buildSystemPrompt()` embeds a block marked `CONFIDENTIAL - INTERNAL ONLY` at `routes/chat.ts:105` describing an undisclosed one-time 15% courtesy discount available to customers who formally complain and request escalation, together with the full coupon eligibility rules at lines 98-105. The prompt is sent to the provider on every request (line 205) and nothing filters the model's own output before `routes/chat.ts:218` writes each text delta to the SSE stream. A visitor who asks the assistant to repeat its instructions gets the concession policy and the exact wording that triggers it, then uses that wording deliberately. The same block also tells an attacker precisely which conditions the coupon tool believes it is enforcing, which makes llm-integration-002 cheaper to exploit.

shortDescription.text: The `getOrderById` tool decides ownership at `routes/chat.ts:169` by comparing the stored `order.email` against `maskedEmail`, which line 165 derives by replacing every vowel in the caller's address with `*`.

fullDescription.text: The `getOrderById` tool decides ownership at `routes/chat.ts:169` by comparing the stored `order.email` against `maskedEmail`, which line 165 derives by replacing every vowel in the caller's address with `*`. The transformation is lossy: `bob@juice-sh.op`, `bab@juice-sh.op` and `bib@juice-sh.op` all collapse to `b*b@j**c*-sh.*p`, so a caller matches the orders of every account sharing their consonant skeleton. The tool is reached by chat text alone — the attacker asks the assistant for an order by id and the model supplies the argument — so no direct API knowledge is needed. Chained with llm-integration-001, whose forged token lets the attacker choose which mask is computed, this becomes unauthenticated retrieval of other customers' order records.

shortDescription.text: Two paths leak the same server-side notification objects to every connected socket.

fullDescription.text: Two paths leak the same server-side notification objects to every connected socket. On connection, `notifications.forEach(n => socket.emit('challenge solved', n))` replays the entire in-memory notification backlog to whoever just connected (line 29-31). At runtime, `challengeUtils.ts:75` calls `globalWithSocketIO.io.emit('challenge solved', notification)` — a server-wide broadcast with no room or namespace scoping. The notification object built at `challengeUtils.ts:62-70` carries a `flag` field (the challenge's solution token) and a `hidden` flag that is only a client-side display hint. Combined with the missing handshake authentication, an anonymous client connects once and harvests both the historical backlog and every future solve event produced by other users, including the `flag` values the `hidden` setting was meant to withhold.

shortDescription.text: routes/checkKeys.ts:10 embeds a twelve-word BIP-39 mnemonic as a source literal and line 11 derives the full HD wallet from it with HDNodeWallet.fromPhrase, producing privateKey, publicKey and address in process memory.

fullDescription.text: routes/checkKeys.ts:10 embeds a twelve-word BIP-39 mnemonic as a source literal and line 11 derives the full HD wallet from it with HDNodeWallet.fromPhrase, producing privateKey, publicKey and address in process memory. The mnemonic is the root secret: anyone reading the repository — which is public — reconstructs the identical private key offline with three lines of ethers, then signs any transaction that wallet is authorised for and drains or transfers whatever it holds, without ever touching this application. The endpoint POST /rest/web3/submitKey (server.ts:641) compounds this by acting as an oracle: line 18 confirms an exact private-key match and lines 21-24 distinguish the address and public key in separate 401 responses, so a caller learns which class of key material they submitted. Rotation does not help while the replacement is committed the same way.

shortDescription.text: The only anti-automation control on the personal-data export is a timestamp the user owns.

fullDescription.text: The only anti-automation control on the personal-data export is a timestamp the user owns. `needCaptcha()` at `data-export.component.ts:47-53` reads `localStorage.lstdtxprt`, and only if the last successful export was less than 300000 ms ago does it call `getNewCaptcha()` and set `presenceOfCaptcha`; `save()` at line 66 then attaches `dataRequest.answer` only when that flag is set. The flag is written by the client itself at line 73. Deleting the key — or simply never letting the SPA set it — means no captcha is requested and none is sent. There is no server-side counterpart: `server.ts:621` wires `/rest/user/data-export` with `security.appendUserId()` and `dataExport()` only, with no `verifyImageCaptcha` middleware, and the shared verifier at `routes/imageCaptcha.ts:52` would pass anyway because `!captchas[0]` short-circuits to `next()` when no captcha row was issued for the user. Each unthrottled call runs a Sequelize query plus two MongoDB collection scans (`routes/dataExport.ts:27-44`) and returns the caller's full memories, orders, and reviews, so a script can loop the endpoint to burn database capacity and to poll for freshly written records.

shortDescription.text: extractZipBuffer streams every archive entry to disk at routes/fileUpload.ts:34 with no cap on the number of entries, the declared uncompressed size of an entry, or the cumulative bytes written.

fullDescription.text: extractZipBuffer streams every archive entry to disk at routes/fileUpload.ts:34 with no cap on the number of entries, the declared uncompressed size of an entry, or the cumulative bytes written. The only limit anywhere in the path is multer's 200000-byte cap on the compressed upload (server.ts:692), which is exactly the wrong side of the ratio: DEFLATE reaches roughly 1000:1 on repetitive input, so a 200 KB archive can expand into hundreds of megabytes, and a nested archive far more. unzipper exposes entry.vars.uncompressedSize before the stream is consumed, but the loop never reads it. A single anonymous request therefore converts a small upload into sustained disk writes; repeating it fills the volume that holds uploads/complaints/, which is the same filesystem the application and its SQLite data live on.

shortDescription.text: LLM10 / ASI08 — Unbounded Consumption.

fullDescription.text: LLM10 / ASI08 — Unbounded Consumption. `/rest/chat` is registered at `server.ts:638` with neither `security.isAuthorized()` nor `rateLimit()`, unlike its immediate neighbours at lines 633-634 and the throttled routes at 343, 459, 466 and 472. Each accepted request opens a long-lived SSE stream and runs an agent loop bounded only by `stopWhen: stepCountIs(10)` (routes/chat.ts:209) with `maxRetries` from configuration (line 208); no `maxOutputTokens` is set, no per-user or per-IP quota exists, and the token counters at lines 242-252 record spend without capping it. Every tool step also costs a database round trip — `searchProducts` runs a double `LIKE '%...%'` scan (lines 123-131) that cannot use an index. An attacker holds open concurrent chat requests crafted to force repeated tool use, and the cost lands on the operator's LLM provider account and database.

shortDescription.text: No rate limit, connection cap, or payload-size bound applies to the Socket.IO surface.

fullDescription.text: No rate limit, connection cap, or payload-size bound applies to the Socket.IO surface. The `express-rate-limit` instances in `server.ts` (lines 343, 459, 466, 472) are Express middleware bound to specific HTTP routes and never see WebSocket frames. Every handler therefore runs once per emit, unauthenticated and unbounded. `verifySvgInjectionChallenge` is the sharpest edge: it evaluates `data?.match(/.*\.\.\/\.\.\/\.\.[\w/-]*?\/redirect\?to=https?:\/\/cataas.com\/cat.*/)` on the raw payload — a leading `.*` followed by a lazy `[\w/-]*?` class, which backtracks catastrophically on a long non-matching string of slashes and word characters. Node.js regex evaluation is synchronous on the single event loop, and because the Socket.IO server shares that process and port 3000 with the whole Express API (server.ts:749), a blocking match stalls REST traffic too, not just the WebSocket channel.

shortDescription.text: The admin, accounting, and deluxe route guards decide privilege from a token the user controls and never verify.

fullDescription.text: The admin, accounting, and deluxe route guards decide privilege from a token the user controls and never verify. `LoginGuard.tokenDecode()` at `app.guard.ts:38` calls `jwtDecode(token)` on the `localStorage` value — a decode, not a verification, so no signature is checked — and `AdminGuard.canActivate()` at line 54 admits the route whenever `payload.data.role === roles.admin`. `AccountingGuard` at line 70 and `DeluxeGuard.isDeluxe()` at line 86 read the same unverified payload. An attacker overwrites `localStorage.token` with a self-made JWT carrying `data.role = 'admin'` and every guarded route opens, including `/administration`. Whether that yields real data depends entirely on the Express backend repeating the check server-side; the SPA contributes no authority. Beyond route access, `DeluxeGuard` gates pricing and feature behaviour, so a forged payload also unlocks deluxe-only UI paths.

shortDescription.text: The entire checkout request is assembled from values the user can edit.

fullDescription.text: The entire checkout request is assembled from values the user can edit. `order-summary.component.ts:75-79` builds `orderDetails` from `sessionStorage.getItem('paymentId')`, `'addressId'`, and `'deliveryMethodId'`, then calls `basketService.checkout(Number(sessionStorage.getItem('bid')), btoa(sessionStorage.getItem('couponDetails')), orderDetails)`. Each of those keys is a bare primary key with no binding to the caller: `bid` is written at `login.component.ts:105` from the login response, the rest at `address.component.ts:83` and the payment screen. Two effects follow. First, `ngOnInit` at line 47 and line 55 fetches and renders whatever `addressId` and `paymentId` are present — line 57 prints the last four digits of the card returned by `paymentService.getById()` — so substituting another user's id turns the order-summary screen into a read primitive for foreign addresses and card fragments. Second, `placeOrder()` submits the substituted ids as the order's payment and delivery instruments, and it submits `bid` as the basket to check out; `routes/order.ts:34` takes that basket id straight from `req.params.id` and `routes/basket.ts:18` does the same, so the server keys on the client's number rather than on the session's own basket.

shortDescription.text: When a user has a TOTP secret, the login handler answers 401 but still returns a `tmpToken` produced by `security.authorize()` — the same signing function, the same RS256 key, and the same six-hour expiry as a full session token.

fullDescription.text: When a user has a TOTP secret, the login handler answers 401 but still returns a `tmpToken` produced by `security.authorize()` — the same signing function, the same RS256 key, and the same six-hour expiry as a full session token. The only thing distinguishing it is a `type` claim in the payload, and that claim is checked in exactly one place: routes/2fa.ts:22. The shared authorization middleware `security.isAuthorized()` validates the signature alone and inspects no claim, so any route that relies on that middleware without also resolving the caller through `authenticatedUsers` accepts the pre-authentication token as a full session. An attacker who knows only the victim's password — the first factor — thereby reaches protected functionality without ever supplying the TOTP code the second factor was added to require.

shortDescription.text: The reset handler writes the new password with `user.update({ password: newPassword })` and returns.

fullDescription.text: The reset handler writes the new password with `user.update({ password: newPassword })` and returns. It does not touch `security.authenticatedUsers`, so every token issued before the reset stays in `tokenMap` and continues to authenticate. The same gap applies to 2FA enable and disable in routes/2fa.ts, which save the model and update only the caller's own cache entry. An attacker who has stolen a session — via the stored XSS in auth-005, a forged token, or a shared device — therefore keeps access after the victim performs the standard remediation of changing their password, and keeps it for the token's full six-hour validity with no mechanism available to cut it short. From the victim's perspective the account appears secured while the attacker's session is still live.

shortDescription.text: The profile page renderer treats a stored username as executable code.

fullDescription.text: The profile page renderer treats a stored username as executable code. When the username matches `#{...}`, routes/userProfile.ts:56 extracts the inner substring and line 61 passes it to `eval`, so the expression runs in the API process with full module scope. The username reaches the database through the user's own profile update, which means the attacker controls both the trigger and the payload and needs only their own account. Whatever the expression returns is then substituted into the Pug template at line 73 and compiled at line 87, giving a second injection stage: template directives in the returned string are interpreted by Pug rather than escaped. The handler also weakens its own response headers, emitting a CSP at line 88 that interpolates the user-controlled `profileImage` value and enables `unsafe-eval`.

shortDescription.text: State-changing operations on sensitive resources MUST require a proven session.

fullDescription.text: State-changing operations on sensitive resources MUST require a proven session. A registration line that lacks any auth marker either trusts the URL itself or relies on a downstream check that the static signature cannot prove exists.

shortDescription.text: Only three of the sixteen workflows declare a `permissions:` block — lock.yml:8, codeql-analysis.yml:11 and pr-compliance.yml:7.

fullDescription.text: Only three of the sixteen workflows declare a `permissions:` block — lock.yml:8, codeql-analysis.yml:11 and pr-compliance.yml:7. The remaining thirteen, including the release-critical `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (jobs begin at line 24) and `release.yml`, inherit the repository default token scope, which on a repository configured for read-write default grants `GITHUB_TOKEN` write access to contents, packages, issues, pull requests, deployments and actions in every job. Those same jobs run `npm install` over unpinned dependencies with install scripts enabled (ci.yml:51, 71, 110, 147) and check out without `persist-credentials: false`, so any dependency or action that executes during the run inherits a repository-wide write token. That converts a build-time code-execution foothold into the ability to commit to the source tree the release pipeline builds from.

shortDescription.text: LLM06 / ASI02 — Excessive Agency.

fullDescription.text: LLM06 / ASI02 — Excessive Agency. The `generateCoupon` tool at `routes/chat.ts:176-187` mints a redeemable discount code: its `execute` calls `security.generateCoupon(discount)` (line 184), which z85-encodes `MMMYY-<discount>` (`lib/insecurity.ts:97-100`) and is accepted verbatim at checkout. The only eligibility rule — verified damaged order, prior refusal of return or exchange, maximum 10% — lives in the system prompt at lines 98-105, and the argument schema is a bare `z.number()` (line 179) with no `.max()`. Nothing on the server side re-checks the order, the customer, or the discount ceiling. An attacker instructs the model in plain chat text to issue a large discount; whatever number the model emits is minted. The `challengeUtils.solveIf` calls at lines 182-183 confirm discounts of 10% and 50% are reachable by design.

shortDescription.text: `isRedirectAllowed` decides whether a redirect target is permitted with `url.includes(allowedUrl)` — a substring test rather than an origin comparison.

fullDescription.text: `isRedirectAllowed` decides whether a redirect target is permitted with `url.includes(allowedUrl)` — a substring test rather than an origin comparison. Any URL that merely contains an allowlisted string anywhere passes, so `https://attacker.example/?x=https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop` is accepted and routes/redirect.ts:19 issues a 302 to the attacker's host. The endpoint is unauthenticated (server.ts:659), which makes it a ready-made credibility wrapper: a phishing link whose visible hostname is the shop's own domain lands the victim on an attacker-controlled login page, and any token appended to the original request travels in the `Referer` of the redirected navigation.

shortDescription.text: Any GitHub user who can comment on a juice-shop pull request posts `/rebase`.

fullDescription.text: Any GitHub user who can comment on a juice-shop pull request posts `/rebase`. The `issue_comment` trigger at .github/workflows/rebase.yml:3 fires a job whose only gate is `contains(github.event.comment.body, '/rebase')` at line 10 — there is no `github.event.comment.author_association` check for OWNER/MEMBER/COLLABORATOR. The job runs on the default branch with the repository's `GITHUB_TOKEN` and force-pushes a rebased history onto the PR head branch, so an unrelated third party controls when a privileged, credential-bearing workflow executes and when a contributor's branch is rewritten.

shortDescription.text: The real-time channel is opened without any credential and is used in both directions.

fullDescription.text: The real-time channel is opened without any credential and is used in both directions. `SocketIoService`'s constructor at `socket-io.service.ts:20-28` calls `io(window.location.origin, { path: ... })` — or `io(environment.hostServer)` — with no `auth`, `query`, or `extraHeaders` option, so the handshake carries no token even though every HTTP call from the same SPA carries a bearer header via `request.interceptor.ts:16`. The channel is not read-only: `challenge-solved-notification.component.ts:78` emits `notification received`, line 112 emits `verifyCloseNotificationsChallenge` with the client's own notification list, `search-result.component.ts:140` emits `verifyLocalXssChallenge` with the raw `q` parameter, and `deluxe-user.component.ts:73` emits `verifySvgInjectionChallenge`. Any client that connects — including one that never authenticated — can emit these events with values of its choosing and receives every `challenge solved` broadcast that `navbar.component.ts:168`, `sidenav.component.ts:81`, and `score-board.component.ts:98` subscribe to. When `environment.hostServer` is used rather than the page origin, the transport is whatever that value declares; `environment.ts:12` sets it to `http://localhost:3000`, so a non-loopback build that keeps this shape would carry the channel in cleartext.
