fullDescription.text: MD5/SHA-1 are collision-broken; used for passwords they are trivially cracked, and for integrity of attacker-influenced data they are forgeable.

shortDescription.text: `.github/workflows/update-news-www.yml:19` interpolates `${{ github.event.release.tag_name }}` and `${{ github.event.release.published_at }}` directly into a `sed -i 's/.../.../'` command inside a `run:` block.

fullDescription.text: `.github/workflows/update-news-www.yml:19` interpolates `${{ github.event.release.tag_name }}` and `${{ github.event.release.published_at }}` directly into a `sed -i 's/.../.../'` command inside a `run:` block. GitHub expands these expressions textually before the shell sees the line, so a release tag containing a single quote and a shell metacharacter breaks out of the `sed` argument and executes as the runner user. The job checks out `juice-shop/juice-shop.github.io` using `secrets.BOT_TOKEN` at line 14, so the injected command runs next to a credential with write access to a second repository. `.github/workflows/update-news-www-legacy.yml:19` carries the identical construct.

shortDescription.text: POST /rest/web3/walletExploitAddress reads req.body.walletAddress at routes/web3Wallet.ts:15 and adds it to the walletsConnected registry at line 16 — before the try block, before any authentication, and with no format check (a grep of the component for isAddress, joi, zod or validate returns zero hits).

fullDescription.text: POST /rest/web3/walletExploitAddress reads req.body.walletAddress at routes/web3Wallet.ts:15 and adds it to the walletsConnected registry at line 16 — before the try block, before any authentication, and with no format check (a grep of the component for isAddress, joi, zod or validate returns zero hits). The registry is then used at line 27 as the authority for who is credited when the ContractExploited event fires on-chain: walletsConnected.has(exploiter) decides whether the challenge is solved. Two integrity problems follow. First, arbitrary non-address strings enter a security-relevant set, so the correlation key space is attacker-shaped rather than a validated 20-byte address. Second, an attacker can pre-register any third party's address and have the server attribute that party's independent on-chain activity to the attacker's request, because nothing links the registered address to the caller who registered it.

shortDescription.text: Every outgoing request carries a second, unauthenticated statement of who the caller is.

fullDescription.text: Every outgoing request carries a second, unauthenticated statement of who the caller is. `request.interceptor.ts:20-25` reads the `email` key straight out of `localStorage` and attaches it as an `X-User-Email` header, independent of the `Authorization` header built four lines above. The value is not derived from the verified session — it is whatever string the user last put in browser storage, and any user can set it in the console. The server side already has a reader for it: `userEmailFrom()` at `lib/insecurity.ts:93` returns `headers['x-user-email']` with no cross-check against the JWT subject. A grep across `routes/`, `lib/`, and `server.ts` finds no current caller of that helper, so today the header is inert; the exposure is that the SPA supplies a forgeable identity claim as ambient request context, and the first log line, analytics event, or authorization branch that reads it inherits an attacker-chosen identity. Attribution for any action recorded from that header is therefore unusable as evidence — the account named in the record is not necessarily the account that acted.

shortDescription.text: No security event on the authentication surface is recorded.

fullDescription.text: No security event on the authentication surface is recorded. A failed login returns a 401 body and nothing else; a successful login writes only an in-memory map entry; a password reset returns the updated user; 2FA enable and disable write the model and return an empty 200. A grep for any logger call across routes/login.ts, routes/2fa.ts, routes/resetPassword.ts, routes/saveLoginIp.ts and lib/insecurity.ts returns zero hits. The consequence is that a credential-stuffing run, a successful account takeover through the security-question reset, and an attacker disabling a victim's second factor all leave the system with no record naming the actor, the source address, or the time. Incident response cannot establish which accounts were reached, and a user disputing a transaction cannot be contradicted by evidence.

shortDescription.text: Security-relevant state changes in this component leave no attributable record.

fullDescription.text: Security-relevant state changes in this component leave no attributable record. The password update at routes/changePassword.ts:51, the security-answer-based reset at routes/resetPassword.ts:44, the 2FA disable at routes/2fa.ts:162, and the role assignment performed through the generic user endpoint all complete without writing an audit entry naming the actor, the target, the source address, and the outcome. `lib/logger.ts` exists and is used elsewhere for operational messages, but no route imports it for these transitions. The only record of activity is the Morgan HTTP access log at server.ts:338, which captures request lines rather than authorization decisions, is not tamper-evident, and is itself readable and therefore modifiable in the same trust zone. After an account takeover through any of the paths above, no evidence exists to distinguish the legitimate owner from the attacker or to establish when control changed hands.

shortDescription.text: Three workflows write to branches directly from CI under a shared bot identity, and none of them signs the resulting commit.

fullDescription.text: Three workflows write to branches directly from CI under a shared bot identity, and none of them signs the resulting commit. `.github/workflows/frontend-bundle-analysis.yml:59-66` configures `user.name "GitHub Action"`, checks out master and runs `git push origin master` — with `continue-on-error: true` at line 67, so a failed or rejected push leaves no red build. `.github/workflows/lint-fixer.yml:22` and the four `update-*` workflows commit as `JuiceShopBot` via git-auto-commit-action. The only integrity marker used is `commit_options: '--signoff'`, which is an unverified text trailer, not a cryptographic signature, and no workflow configures a GPG or SSH signing key. When a commit later turns out to be malicious, the audit trail cannot distinguish a legitimate bot run from an attacker who obtained the same token, and the `continue-on-error` push hides the attempt entirely.

shortDescription.text: routes/fileUpload.ts imports no logger and emits no log record anywhere in its 140 lines: handleZipFileUpload (line 39) extracts an archive to disk, handleXmlUpload parses attacker XML, and handleYamlUpload evaluates attacker YAML, and none of the three records what was uploaded, what filenames were written, or from which address.

fullDescription.text: routes/fileUpload.ts imports no logger and emits no log record anywhere in its 140 lines: handleZipFileUpload (line 39) extracts an archive to disk, handleXmlUpload parses attacker XML, and handleYamlUpload evaluates attacker YAML, and none of the three records what was uploaded, what filenames were written, or from which address. routes/profileImageFileUpload.ts logs only a failed write (line 45) and nothing about a successful one. Combined with the absent authentication on the endpoint (file-upload-service-002) there is no principal to attribute an upload to and no record that it happened, so after a Zip Slip overwrite or an XXE probe an incident responder has only the metrics counter and whatever files remain on disk. Deletion of the extracted artefact removes the last trace, making the action effectively deniable.

shortDescription.text: Nothing in the Socket.IO registration path writes to the application logger.

fullDescription.text: Nothing in the Socket.IO registration path writes to the application logger. The module imports `config`, `utils`, `socket.io`, `datacache`, `challengeUtils` and `insecurity`, but not `lib/logger`, and a search for `logger`, `winston` and `audit` across the file returns nothing. Connections, disconnections, the state-deleting `notification received` event and the three state-changing `verify*` events all execute silently. Combined with the absent handshake identity, this means the two mutations recorded in findings socket-io-gateway-003 and socket-io-gateway-004 leave no record of what changed, when, or from which source — there is no server-side artefact to distinguish a legitimate dismissal from an attacker emptying the queue, and an incident responder has only the reverse proxy's connection log to work from.

shortDescription.text: Nothing in the data layer records who changed what.

fullDescription.text: Nothing in the data layer records who changed what. `logging: false` at models/index.ts:42 discards the SQL stream entirely, and no model carries an actor column — a grep across `models/` for `createdBy`, `updatedBy`, `audit`, or a logger import returns nothing. Sequelize's default `createdAt`/`updatedAt` timestamps say a row moved but not who moved it. The gap is sharpest on `Wallet.balance` (models/wallet.ts:35), which is a mutable scalar rather than an append-only ledger: a balance can be rewritten in place and the prior value is gone, so a fraudulent top-up is indistinguishable from a legitimate one after the fact and there is no sum-of-entries invariant to reconcile against. The same applies to `role` changes on Users and to soft-deletes under `paranoid: true`. Practically this means the elevation and tampering findings above are not just exploitable but unprovable afterwards: an incident responder cannot establish which account was promoted, when, or by whom, and a disputing customer cannot be contradicted.

shortDescription.text: LLM07 — internal detail exposure through an ineffective debug guard.

fullDescription.text: LLM07 — internal detail exposure through an ineffective debug guard. `routes/chat.ts:228-238` writes every `tool-call` event to the SSE stream, emitting the internal tool name and the model-chosen arguments as JSON. The `show_tool_calls` cookie and the non-admin role test on lines 221-226 sit inside `challengeUtils.solveIf`, which only records a challenge solve — neither value gates the `res.write` that follows, so the exposure applies to every caller including anonymous ones. An attacker watching the stream learns the tool inventory (`searchProducts`, `getProductReviews`, `getOrderById`, `generateCoupon`), the exact argument names, and whether a probing message actually reached the coupon tool. That converts blind prompt-injection attempts against llm-integration-002 into a feedback-driven loop.

shortDescription.text: The User model is declared `paranoid: true` (models/user.ts:123), so Sequelize turns every delete into an UPDATE that sets `deletedAt` and leaves the row intact.

fullDescription.text: The User model is declared `paranoid: true` (models/user.ts:123), so Sequelize turns every delete into an UPDATE that sets `deletedAt` and leaves the row intact. Everything the account held stays in the table indefinitely: email address, password digest, `totpSecret`, `lastLoginIp`, and — through the foreign keys wired in models/relations.ts — the associated Addresses, Cards, and Memories, none of which are cascaded or scrubbed. The erasure path that should compensate does not exist: `models/privacyRequests.ts:34` stores a single `deletionRequested` boolean with a default of `false` and no state machine, no completion timestamp, and no worker that acts on it. So a user exercising a deletion right produces a flag and nothing more. The security consequence is concrete rather than merely regulatory — every later breach of this database exposes the personal data of users who believed they had left years earlier, and the retained `totpSecret` and card rows of deleted accounts are as usable to an attacker as those of active ones.

shortDescription.text: Every handler in this component ends its catch block with res.status(500).json(utils.getErrorMessage(error)), and utils.getErrorMessage (lib/utils.ts:210) returns error.message verbatim with no sanitisation.

fullDescription.text: Every handler in this component ends its catch block with res.status(500).json(utils.getErrorMessage(error)), and utils.getErrorMessage (lib/utils.ts:210) returns error.message verbatim with no sanitisation. The errors reaching that catch originate from the ethers WebSocketProvider constructed at routes/nftMint.ts:18 and routes/web3Wallet.ts:20, whose endpoint URL embeds the server's third-party credential: wss://eth-sepolia.g.alchemy.com/v2/${process.env.ALCHEMY_API_KEY}. Provider and transport errors routinely quote the connection target, so an anonymous caller who triggers a failure — the endpoints need no authentication — can receive the Alchemy API key or, at minimum, the internal provider topology, dependency versions and failure modes. Because the same handler logs the message at line 20, the credential can also land in application logs and any downstream log sink.

shortDescription.text: `authenticatedUsers.put()` writes each issued token into two process-global objects, `tokenMap` keyed by the full JWT string and `idMap` keyed by user id.

fullDescription.text: `authenticatedUsers.put()` writes each issued token into two process-global objects, `tokenMap` keyed by the full JWT string and `idMap` keyed by user id. Nothing ever removes an entry: there is no logout handler, no expiry sweep tied to the token's 6-hour lifetime, and no size bound — a repository-wide grep for token deletion or a logout route returns zero hits. Every successful login therefore adds a permanent entry holding the complete user object. An attacker with any working credential — or with the login SQL injection, which needs none — drives repeated logins and grows the map without limit until the Node heap is exhausted and the process dies, taking the whole single-process application down. The same absence means a stolen token stays honoured in the cache for its full lifetime with no way to revoke it.

shortDescription.text: `extractZipBuffer` iterates every entry of an uploaded archive and streams each one to disk with no bound on entry count, per-entry uncompressed size, or cumulative output.

fullDescription.text: `extractZipBuffer` iterates every entry of an uploaded archive and streams each one to disk with no bound on entry count, per-entry uncompressed size, or cumulative output. The upload itself is capped at 200 KB by multer (server.ts:692), but that cap applies to the compressed input; a 200 KB zip of highly redundant data expands to many gigabytes. Because the loop awaits each `pipeline` sequentially and never checks free space or an aggregate byte counter, a single anonymous POST to `/file-upload` fills the volume backing `uploads/`, which is the same filesystem that holds the SQLite database and the log files. Repeated posts also hold the event loop in filesystem work.

shortDescription.text: handleYamlUpload evaluates yaml.load(data) inside a vm context at routes/fileUpload.ts:109 with `{ timeout: 2000 }`.

fullDescription.text: handleYamlUpload evaluates yaml.load(data) inside a vm context at routes/fileUpload.ts:109 with `{ timeout: 2000 }`. A vm timeout bounds wall-clock execution but not heap allocation, and V8 does not interrupt a running allocation to honour it - a billion-laughs YAML document whose nested aliases multiply out to gigabytes drives the Node process toward its heap limit before the 2000 ms deadline can take effect. The catch block on lines 114-119 already anticipates this by matching 'Invalid string length' and marking a yamlBomb challenge solved, which confirms the expansion runs to completion rather than being pre-empted. Since the endpoint is anonymous, a handful of concurrent requests can push the single Node process into an out-of-memory abort, taking the whole shop down rather than only the upload feature.

shortDescription.text: The datastore is an in-process SQLite file, so the database shares the Node event loop and the container's disk with the application it serves.

fullDescription.text: The datastore is an in-process SQLite file, so the database shares the Node event loop and the container's disk with the application it serves. SQLite allows one writer at a time; the configuration at models/index.ts:35-40 acknowledges this by retrying on `SQLITE_BUSY` at most five times and by forcing `Transaction.TYPES.IMMEDIATE`, which takes the write lock at transaction start rather than at first write and therefore widens the window during which every other writer is blocked. There is no `busyTimeout`, no statement timeout, and no pool cap. The consequence is that write concurrency is bounded by retry count rather than by a queue: a modest burst of concurrent writes — bulk feedback posts, repeated basket updates, a scripted registration flood — exhausts five retries and surfaces as request failures for unrelated users, not just for the attacker. Because the file is local and unbounded, the same write path also lets an attacker grow the database on disk until the volume fills, at which point every write across the application fails at once.

shortDescription.text: routes/web3Wallet.ts:16 executes walletsConnected.add(req.body.walletAddress) on every call to POST /rest/web3/walletExploitAddress, unconditionally and before the try block.

fullDescription.text: routes/web3Wallet.ts:16 executes walletsConnected.add(req.body.walletAddress) on every call to POST /rest/web3/walletExploitAddress, unconditionally and before the try block. The Set is process-global (line 10), entries are only ever removed when a matching ContractExploited event arrives on-chain (line 28), and nothing caps its size, expires entries or validates that the value is even an address. The route carries no authentication and no rate limiting — the component contains zero rateLimit references and server.ts applies express-rate-limit only to /rest/user/reset-password. An anonymous attacker therefore loops the endpoint with distinct large strings and grows heap allocation until the Node process degrades or is OOM-killed, taking the whole shop down rather than just this feature. The addressesMinted Set at routes/nftMint.ts:10 has the same unbounded shape, fed by chain events rather than requests.

shortDescription.text: Three handlers — `verifyLocalXssChallenge`, `verifySvgInjectionChallenge`, `verifyCloseNotificationsChallenge` (lines 40-51) — let the client's own payload decide whether a server-side challenge is marked solved.

fullDescription.text: Three handlers — `verifyLocalXssChallenge`, `verifySvgInjectionChallenge`, `verifyCloseNotificationsChallenge` (lines 40-51) — let the client's own payload decide whether a server-side challenge is marked solved. Each passes `data` straight into `challengeUtils.solveIf(...)`, whose predicate is a pure string comparison or a regex over that payload; nothing corroborates that the described action actually happened in the browser. `verifyCloseNotificationsChallenge` is the extreme case: the predicate is `Array.isArray(data) && data.length > 1`, so emitting a two-element array is the whole exploit. Because the socket has no identity, an anonymous client drives a privileged application state transition that `solveIf` propagates into the persisted challenge record and the global solve broadcast, attributing progress that the caller never earned and was never authenticated to claim.

shortDescription.text: GET /rest/web3/nftMintListen is registered at server.ts:643 with no security.isAuthorized() middleware, and the handler at routes/nftMint.ts:17-29 makes the server open an outbound WebSocket to Alchemy using its own ALCHEMY_API_KEY and register a persistent NFTMinted contract listener at line 24.

fullDescription.text: GET /rest/web3/nftMintListen is registered at server.ts:643 with no security.isAuthorized() middleware, and the handler at routes/nftMint.ts:17-29 makes the server open an outbound WebSocket to Alchemy using its own ALCHEMY_API_KEY and register a persistent NFTMinted contract listener at line 24. An anonymous internet caller therefore drives a privileged, credentialed backend action they hold no authority for: the listener is process-global, survives the request, and consumes the operator's third-party API quota. The isEventListenerCreated flag is reset to false on any transport error (line 21), so an attacker who can force provider errors can re-trigger creation repeatedly and multiply connections and quota burn. This is the same gap across the whole /rest/web3/* surface — none of the five routes at server.ts:641-645 carries an authentication guard, so the boundary assumption that state-changing routes sit behind expressJwt does not hold here.

message.text: The User model's `password` attribute setter is the single place where every credential in the system is transformed before storage. It calls `security.hash(clearTextPassword)`, which is an unsalted MD5 digest (`lib/insecurity.ts:41`). Because the setter is on the model rather than in a route, every write path — registration, password reset, admin-created accounts, seed data — inherits it, so there is no code path that stores a stronger digest. Two properties make the stored column directly usable to an attacker: MD5 is a fast, GPU-friendly hash with no work factor, and the absence of a per-row salt means identical passwords produce identical digests, so a single rainbow table covers the whole Users table at once. Any read primitive over the database — SQL injection, a leaked backup, a file-read on the co-located SQLite file — converts immediately into cleartext credentials rather than into a cracking problem that costs the attacker time.

message.text: The repository disables lockfiles outright — the root `.npmrc` and `frontend/.npmrc` both contain a lockfile-disabling directive, `package-lock.json` is listed in `.gitignore:10`, and neither `package-lock.json` nor `frontend/package-lock.json` exists in the tree. Every build therefore resolves the semver ranges in `package.json` fresh against the registry: `Dockerfile:5` runs `npm install --omit=dev`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml:51` and every test job run bare `npm install`, and `npm ci` appears nowhere in the repository. An attacker who publishes a malicious patch release of any direct or transitive dependency — or who compromises an existing maintainer account — is picked up automatically by the next build. Because `npm install` executes `postinstall` scripts and the docker job publishes the result to `bkimminich/juice-shop:latest` (ci.yml:345), that package's code runs on the runner holding `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` and ships inside the published image to every downstream consumer.

message.text: The SPA is the token custodian for the whole system. `login.component.ts:101` receives the raw JWT in the login response body and hands it to browser storage; `request.interceptor.ts:16` then attaches it to every direct call the browser makes to `/api` and `/rest`. No server-side session broker sits between the browser and the API, so the browser holds a long-lived credential that JavaScript must be able to read by design — which is why the storage and guard weaknesses in this component escalate to account takeover rather than staying UI defects. The same architecture forces the SPA to inspect the token itself (`app.guard.ts:38`), leaks the credential into the OAuth URL fragment (`login.component.ts:148`), and leaves nothing to revoke server-side when a token is stolen. A Backend-for-Frontend removes the class: the Express tier exchanges credentials, keeps the API token server-side, and issues the browser only an opaque `HttpOnly` session cookie.

message.text: The whole datastore is a single plain file — `storage: 'data/juiceshop.sqlite'` — created by the stock `sequelize` sqlite dialect with no page passphrase and no SQLCipher build. It sits inside the application's own working directory, which is also the directory tree the application serves files from, so a path-traversal or arbitrary-file-read primitive anywhere in the shop reads the entire database in one request rather than one row at a time. What that file holds makes the difference material: `models/card.ts:38` stores `cardNum` as a full unmasked `INTEGER` primary account number with no tokenisation or truncation, and `models/user.ts:112` stores `totpSecret` as a plain `STRING` — the shared seed that generates second-factor codes. Neither field is encrypted at the column level either, so there is no defence-in-depth behind the missing file encryption. An attacker who obtains the file gets card numbers they can charge and TOTP seeds that defeat the second factor, without needing to break any cryptography.

message.text: An attacker who knows any Google-login user's email address can authenticate as that user without touching Google. On the OAuth callback, `oauth.component.ts:30` computes `const password = btoa(profile.email.split('').reverse().join(''))` and registers the account with it via `userService.save()`, then `login()` at line 46 reuses the same derivation to sign in through the ordinary `/rest/user/login` password endpoint. The derivation is a public, deterministic function of a public identifier: base64 of the reversed email. Every OAuth account therefore also has a working local password that the attacker can compute offline, which makes the password endpoint a parallel authentication path around the federated flow entirely — MFA, Google account recovery, and the `authorizedRedirects` allowlist all sit on the other path and never see the request.

message.text: The RSA private key used to sign every session JWT is a literal PEM block in `lib/insecurity.ts`, committed to a public repository. `authorize()` signs with that constant and the matching public key ships as `encryptionkeys/jwt.pub`, so the signing secret is available to anyone who can read the source or pull the published container image. An attacker constructs a payload of their choosing — `{"data": {"id": 1, "email": "admin@juice-sh.op", "role": "admin"}}` — signs it with the copied key using RS256, and presents it as a Bearer token. Every server-side check that only verifies the signature accepts it. The same constant is reused as the HMAC key for `deluxeToken()` at line 150, so the deluxe-membership token that `isDeluxe()` cross-checks is forgeable from the same material.

message.text: Every server-side token check omits an algorithm allow-list. `isAuthorized()` constructs the express-jwt middleware with only `{ secret: publicKey }`; `updateAuthenticatedUsers()` on line 189 calls `jwt.verify(token, publicKey, cb)` with no options object; and `verify()` on line 55 hands the public key to `jws.verify` in the algorithm parameter. The pinned dependency versions — express-jwt 0.1.3 and jsonwebtoken 0.4.0 in package.json — predate algorithm enforcement, so the header's `alg` field decides which verification routine runs. An attacker sets the header algorithm to `none`, strips the signature, and supplies an arbitrary payload; alternatively they switch to a symmetric HMAC algorithm and sign with the published `encryptionkeys/jwt.pub` contents, which the code passes as the verification secret. Both variants yield a token the middleware treats as authentic.

message.text: The login handler builds its credential lookup by string interpolation: the raw `req.body.email` value is pasted into a `SELECT * FROM Users WHERE email = '...' AND password = '...'` statement and executed through Sequelize's raw-query API with `plain: true`. An unauthenticated attacker posting `{"email": "' OR 1=1--", "password": "x"}` to POST /rest/user/login terminates the email literal and comments out the entire password comparison, so the query returns the first row of the Users table. The handler then treats that row as a verified user and calls `security.authorize()` on it, minting a signed 6-hour RS256 JWT for whichever account is returned — in the seeded dataset, the admin. The same primitive supports UNION-based extraction of every column of the Users table, including the MD5 password hashes and TOTP secrets.

Because `plain: true` returns exactly one row and the seeded admin is row 1, the attacker receives a valid RS256 JWT for the administrator without ever knowing a password. message.text: POST /rest/user/login accepts unlimited attempts. The route is registered with no rate limiter — unlike /rest/user/reset-password and the three /rest/2fa endpoints, which each carry an express-rate-limit instance — and the handler itself implements no failed-attempt counter, no per-account lockout, no exponential backoff, and no CAPTCHA. An attacker therefore runs credential stuffing against the full user list obtained from routes/authenticatedUsers.ts at whatever rate the network allows, and each attempt costs the server only one MD5 computation, so there is no natural throttle either. Because no authentication event is logged, the campaign is also invisible.

message.text: The middleware chain for POST /file-upload (server.ts:309) is uploadToMemory.single('file') -> ensureFileIsPassed -> observeFileUploadMetricsMiddleware -> checkUploadSize -> checkFileType -> handleZipFileUpload -> handleXmlUpload -> handleYamlUpload. message.text: The Socket.IO server is created with `new Server(server, { cors: { origin: 'http://localhost:4200' } })` and immediately registers `io.on('connection', ...)` with no `io.use()` handshake middleware. Nothing reads `socket.handshake.auth`, `socket.handshake.headers.cookie`, or the JWT that `security.isAuthorized()` validates on the REST side, so the socket never acquires an identity. Because the Socket.IO server is attached to the same HTTP server as the Express API (server.ts:749), an anonymous internet client that can reach port 3000 can open the WebSocket upgrade and immediately invoke every registered event handler. The CORS `origin` value is not a substitute: Socket.IO only enforces it against browsers that send an `Origin` header, and any non-browser client (curl, socket.io-client, a script) connects regardless. This is the WebSocket leg of the same trust boundary the REST API guards with expressJwt.

message.text: Security answers are the fallback authenticator for the password-reset flow, so a digest an attacker can invert is equivalent to a stored password. The SecurityAnswer model protects them with `security.hmac(answer)`, which is HMAC-SHA256 under the literal key `pa4qacea4VK9t9nGv7yZtwmj` compiled into `lib/insecurity.ts:42`. Three defects compound here. The key is a source-code constant in a public repository, so it provides no secrecy against anyone who can read the project. HMAC-SHA256 is a single fast round with no work factor, so it is a poor choice for a low-entropy secret regardless of key handling. And the construction is deterministic without a per-row salt, so equal answers yield equal digests and one precomputed table covers every user. Security answers draw from a small space — a pet name, a city, a mother's maiden name — so a wordlist of a few hundred thousand entries inverts essentially the whole SecurityAnswers table.

Second, an attacker can pre-register any third party's address and have the server attribute that party's independent on-chain activity to the attacker's request, because nothing links the registered address to the caller who registered it.

message.text: The User model is declared `paranoid: true` (models/user.ts:123), so Sequelize turns every delete into an UPDATE that sets `deletedAt` and leaves the row intact. Everything the account held stays in the table indefinitely: email address, password digest, `totpSecret`, `lastLoginIp`, and — through the foreign keys wired in models/relations.ts — the associated Addresses, Cards, and Memories, none of which are cascaded or scrubbed. The erasure path that should compensate does not exist: `models/privacyRequests.ts:34` stores a single `deletionRequested` boolean with a default of `false` and no state machine, no completion timestamp, and no worker that acts on it. So a user exercising a deletion right produces a flag and nothing more. The security consequence is concrete rather than merely regulatory — every later breach of this database exposes the personal data of users who believed they had left years earlier, and the retained `totpSecret` and card rows of deleted accounts are as usable to an attacker as those of active ones.

message.text: `authenticatedUsers.put()` writes each issued token into two process-global objects, `tokenMap` keyed by the full JWT string and `idMap` keyed by user id. Nothing ever removes an entry: there is no logout handler, no expiry sweep tied to the token's 6-hour lifetime, and no size bound — a repository-wide grep for token deletion or a logout route returns zero hits. Every successful login therefore adds a permanent entry holding the complete user object. An attacker with any working credential — or with the login SQL injection, which needs none — drives repeated logins and grows the map without limit until the Node heap is exhausted and the process dies, taking the whole single-process application down. The same absence means a stolen token stays honoured in the cache for its full lifetime with no way to revoke it.

message.text: `extractZipBuffer` iterates every entry of an uploaded archive and streams each one to disk with no bound on entry count, per-entry uncompressed size, or cumulative output. The upload itself is capped at 200 KB by multer (server.ts:692), but that cap applies to the compressed input; a 200 KB zip of highly redundant data expands to many gigabytes. Because the loop awaits each `pipeline` sequentially and never checks free space or an aggregate byte counter, a single anonymous POST to `/file-upload` fills the volume backing `uploads/`, which is the same filesystem that holds the SQLite database and the log files. Repeated posts also hold the event loop in filesystem work.

message.text: handleYamlUpload evaluates yaml.load(data) inside a vm context at routes/fileUpload.ts:109 with `{ timeout: 2000 }`. A vm timeout bounds wall-clock execution but not heap allocation, and V8 does not interrupt a running allocation to honour it - a billion-laughs YAML document whose nested aliases multiply out to gigabytes drives the Node process toward its heap limit before the 2000 ms deadline can take effect. The catch block on lines 114-119 already anticipates this by matching 'Invalid string length' and marking a yamlBomb challenge solved, which confirms the expansion runs to completion rather than being pre-empted. Since the endpoint is anonymous, a handful of concurrent requests can push the single Node process into an out-of-memory abort, taking the whole shop down rather than only the upload feature.

message.text: The datastore is an in-process SQLite file, so the database shares the Node event loop and the container's disk with the application it serves. SQLite allows one writer at a time; the configuration at models/index.ts:35-40 acknowledges this by retrying on `SQLITE_BUSY` at most five times and by forcing `Transaction.TYPES.IMMEDIATE`, which takes the write lock at transaction start rather than at first write and therefore widens the window during which every other writer is blocked. There is no `busyTimeout`, no statement timeout, and no pool cap. The consequence is that write concurrency is bounded by retry count rather than by a queue: a modest burst of concurrent writes — bulk feedback posts, repeated basket updates, a scripted registration flood — exhausts five retries and surfaces as request failures for unrelated users, not just for the attacker. Because the file is local and unbounded, the same write path also lets an attacker grow the database on disk until the volume fills, at which point every write across the application fails at once.

message.text: Three handlers — `verifyLocalXssChallenge`, `verifySvgInjectionChallenge`, `verifyCloseNotificationsChallenge` (lines 40-51) — let the client's own payload decide whether a server-side challenge is marked solved. Each passes `data` straight into `challengeUtils.solveIf(...)`, whose predicate is a pure string comparison or a regex over that payload; nothing corroborates that the described action actually happened in the browser. `verifyCloseNotificationsChallenge` is the extreme case: the predicate is `Array.isArray(data) && data.length > 1`, so emitting a two-element array is the whole exploit. Because the socket has no identity, an anonymous client drives a privileged application state transition that `solveIf` propagates into the persisted challenge record and the global solve broadcast, attributing progress that the caller never earned and was never authenticated to claim.
